questions.stem: A 57-year-old man presented with a lump on the right side of his neck. He had been feeling well with no systemic symptoms. He had well-controlled diabetes (HbA1C of 6%) and no drug allergies. On physical exam, the lump was nontender and easily moveable. It was not red or hot. He underwent a biopsy to evaluate for malignancy. Investigations: Direct microscopy: inflammatory cells and grampositive branching rods seen Culture: molar tooth-appearing colonies present on anaerobic plates
questions.lead_in: What is the most appropriate treatment?
questions.explanation: Penicillin Microbiology and clinical presentation are consistent with infection by Actinomyces sp. Penicillin is the drug of choice for actinomycosis. Surgical resection is not typically necessary for Actinomyces cervicofacial infections unless there is a complex abscess or unless marsupialization of a fistula were required as antibiotics alone should be curative. If an empyema were present, drainage would be indicated. Doxycycline and clindamycin would be second-line agents and are reserved for cases where the patient has penicillin allergy. TMP–SMX would be used if treating Nocardia, but recall that Nocardia is an aerobic organism. Nocardia would be an unlikely organism in this location unless the patient had a penetrating trauma to the area.
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 1 Q10

questions.stem: A 56-year-old man presented with a slow-growing painless soft tissue swelling of the perimandibular region over 2 months. It had started discharging small amounts of pus through a small opening in the skin 2 weeks earlier. It had responded temporarily to a short course of co-amoxiclav but had then relapsed. He had no weight loss, fever, chills, or other constitutional symptoms. He was otherwise in good health, worked in an office, and had a long-term male partner. He smoked 15 cigarettes a day. There was no history of recent dental work or trauma to the face or mouth. On examination there was a firm 4×5 cm mass in right submandibular region, tender to palpate, and partially fixed on the deep tissue planes. The overlying skin was slightly bluish in color, and there was a small sinus discharging thick yellow exudate. Investigations: CT head/neck: ill-defined mass in the left pyriform fossa involving the perimandibular gland and platysma muscle. Mass is infiltrative, crossing tissue planes. Moderately enhancing with several low attenuating foci. No associated lymphadenopathy A biopsy was performed: Direct microscopy: scanty gram-positive bacilli seen; branching filaments, diphtheroids, and coccobacilli Modified Kinyoun stain negative Bacterial cultures: aerobic, enhanced CO2 and anaerobic cultures negative Fungal cultures: no growth at 25°C or 37°C Histology: chronic inflammation with the presence of multiple granules surrounded by polymorphonuclear leukocytes; an eosinophilic fringe surrounds the PMN zone
questions.lead_in: What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Actinomycosis Actinomycosis is most commonly caused by Actinomyces israelii, which may be a component of normal oropharyngeal flora. This chronic, invasive infection mimics malignancy as it may invade local muscle and bone if left untreated. Sinus tracts may occur. Oral cervicofacial actinomycosis is the commonest presentation, but thoracic and abdominopelvic infections are also seen. Diagnosis is usually by demonstration of gram-positive branching filamentous bacilli and sulfur granules; cultures are rarely positive if broad-spectrum antibiotics have been taken.
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 7 Q50

questions.stem: A 47-year-old man is sent from otolaryngology clinic for evaluation of a chronic left mandibular wound. He has poor dentition and has had multiple tooth extractions. He has, for the last 2 months, had swelling and intermittently draining sinus tracts over the angle of his mandible. Superficial wound cultures have not grown any pathogens. Imaging does not show any signs of mandibular osteomyelitis.
questions.lead_in: First-line antimicrobial therapy for patients with this condition should include treatment with an agent in which of the following antibiotic classes?
questions.explanation: β-lactams Cervicofacial actinomycosis is most often treated with penicillins. A variety of other agents have been used with success, including cephalosporins, carbapenems, clindamycin, tetracyclines, erythromycin, and chloramphenicol.

questions.model_answer:
a) IUD-associated pelvic inflammatory disease with a tubo-ovarian abscess/pelvic mass due to pelvic actinomycosis (branching, beaded gram-positive bacilli).
b) Remove the IUD (send it for culture) and obtain the mass for diagnosis and source control - drainage/aspiration under ultrasound or CT guidance by interventional radiology, or operative drainage/laparoscopy, with material sent for aerobic and anaerobic culture; hospitalize for parenteral broad-spectrum therapy.
c) Intravenous penicillin G (18-24 million units/day, divided q4h) - or IV ampicillin - as the anti-actinomycosis agent, given as part of broad-spectrum parenteral coverage of gonococcus, chlamydia, anaerobes and gram-negative facultative organisms (e.g. ampicillin + clindamycin + gentamicin, with doxycycline for chlamydia).
d) Parenteral therapy for about 2-6 weeks, then oral penicillin V or amoxicillin to complete 6-12 months total for pelvic actinomycosis (drainage may shorten this); the PID/anaerobic component needs 14 days of doxycycline +/- metronidazole.
e) Nothing beyond counselling and observation - Actinomyces-like organisms are seen on Pap smears in 4%-8% of IUD users, their presence has not been equated with pelvic actinomycosis, and removal of the IUD is not necessary in an asymptomatic colonized woman; advise her to report pelvic pain, fever or discharge.
questions.beyond_mandell: Actinomycosis drug, route and 6-12 month duration come from the Mandell Actinomyces chapter/standard practice, not this chapter.

cohort_answer.text: Diagnosis: PID +/- tubo-ovarian abscess, possibly pelvic actinomycosis pending culture. Immediate: Remove the IUD, surgical removal of mass vs IR aspirate with culture. Initial treatment: Empiric CRO 1g IV daily + doxycycline 100mg BID + metronidazole 500mg BID until well enough for oral stepdown, then metro/doxy for 14 days total, plus actino treatment (amoxil or penicillin, technically IV for 14 days then PO stepdown); actino specific: IV PenG x2 weeks then 6-12 months PO. Asymptomatic: counsel and monitor for symptoms, IUD stays in.

questions.model_answer:
a) Pelvic actinomycosis - IUD-associated chronic endometritis/PID with a tubo-ovarian (adnexal) mass.
b) Remove the IUD and send it for culture, and obtain/drain the adnexal mass (image-guided percutaneous or transvaginal drainage, or laparoscopic/operative drainage) with aerobic and anaerobic cultures; admit for parenteral therapy.
c) Intravenous penicillin G 18-24 million units/day divided q4h (or IV ampicillin 2 g q4h) for Actinomyces, within a broad-spectrum parenteral regimen also covering anaerobes, gram-negative facultative organisms, gonococcus and chlamydia (e.g. ampicillin + clindamycin + gentamicin, plus doxycycline).
d) 2-6 weeks IV, then oral penicillin V/amoxicillin to complete 6-12 months, guided by clinical and radiologic resolution; the concomitant PID regimen (doxycycline +/- metronidazole) runs 14 days.
e) Observe - Actinomyces-like organisms on Pap smear occur in 4%-8% of IUD users, do not equate with pelvic actinomycosis, and IUD removal and antibiotics are not required in an asymptomatic woman; counsel about symptoms.

questions.model_answer: a) IUCD-associated pelvic actinomycosis with tubo-ovarian involvement. b) Remove the IUCD and obtain pelvic imaging (CT/MRI); drain any significant purulent collection/abscess. c) High-dose IV penicillin G (18–24 million units/day) as initial therapy, followed by oral penicillin or amoxicillin. d) For this bulky/tissue-invasive disease: 2–6 weeks parenteral therapy then oral therapy to a total of 6–12 months, extended beyond radiographic resolution to minimize relapse (a 14-day penicillin or tetracycline course suffices only for possible early actinomycotic endometritis). e) Asymptomatic Actinomyces-like organisms on Pap have low predictive value — do not remove the IUCD; provide patient education and close follow-up.

questions.model_answer: a) IUCD-associated pelvic actinomycosis with a tubo-ovarian/adnexal mass (branching/filamentous gram-positive rods with an IUCD); clue cells indicate concurrent bacterial vaginosis. b) Remove the IUCD and image/drain the adnexal collection. c) High-dose IV penicillin G. d) 2–6 weeks IV then oral penicillin/amoxicillin to a total of 6–12 months for this bulky disease. e) If uncomplicated (early actinomycotic endometritis without abscess): a 14-day course of a penicillin or a tetracycline.
questions.cohort_conflict: The cohort answer frames this as PID/bacterial vaginosis (Gardnerella) with STI-oriented PID regimens; given the actinomycosis chapter, an IUCD, and branching gram-positive rods with an adnexal mass, the primary diagnosis is pelvic actinomycosis (BV/clue cells being a concurrent finding), so the regimen is high-dose penicillin, not empiric PID therapy.

cohort_answer.text: Diagnosis: PID +/- tubo-ovarian complex/abscess (polymicrobial, often including Gardnerella); clue cells suggest BV, particularly Gardnerella vaginalis. Immediate action: Beta-HCG to rule out ectopic pregnancy; Chlamydia + gonorrhoeae NAAT prior to Rx, screen for other STIs including HIV; empiric Rx. Abx route/regimen: Cefoxitin 2g IV q6h + Doxycycline 100mg IV BID + Metronidazole 500mg PO BID (alternatives: Clindamycin+gentamicin, Ofloxacin+Metronidazole, Levofloxacin+Metronidazole, Amp/Sulbactam+Doxycycline, Cipro+Doxy+metronidazole); outpatient CTX 250mg IM x1 + doxycycline 100mg PO BID x14d +/- flagyl if BV; inpatient Cefotetan 2g IV q12h OR cefoxitin 2g IV q6h + doxycycline. Duration: 14 days if uncomplicated (up to 4-6 weeks for TOA). Uncomplicated treatment: Ceftriaxone 250mg IM x1 + Doxycycline x14d OR Cefoxitin 2g IM x1 + Probenecid 1g PO x1 + Doxycycline x14d (add flagyl given clue cells/BV)

questions.model_answer: a) High-dose, prolonged penicillin is the treatment of choice. For serious/bulky disease: IV penicillin 18–24 million units/day for 2–6 weeks, followed by oral penicillin or amoxicillin for a total of 6–12 months. For low-bulk oral-cervicofacial disease a shortened duration is acceptable and therapy can be initiated with an oral agent. Because head-and-neck companion organisms (e.g., Aggregatibacter actinomycetemcomitans, Eikenella corrodens, Fusobacterium, Capnocytophaga) are frequent coisolates, adding empirical coverage for them (e.g., amoxicillin-clavulanate) during initial treatment is reasonable.

questions.beyond_mandell: Only the Sporothrix cigar-shaped yeast morphology is grounded in the slice (p. 3134); the other identifications are standard microbiology.

cohort_answer.text:
Image 1: Leishmania spp. amastigotes, H&E stain - spherical to ovoid, 1-5 µm long by 1-2 µm wide, large nucleus, prominent kinetoplast, short axoneme (rarely visible by light microscopy); reside in macrophages.
Image 2: Nocardia - branching, filamentous, beaded, gram-positive rods with right angle branching (compare/contrast with Rhodococcus equi).
Image 3: Francisella tularensis - tiny, gram-negative coccobacilli, no growth on MacConkey; 'junky' gram stain of tiny GNCB's, DDx Francisella or Brucella; oxidase negative, urease negative, weakly catalase positive, strict aerobes.
Image 4: Sporothrix schenckii - small (~2 microns); PAS stained tissue section showing budding yeast-like cells; conidiophores and conidia are ovoid, elongated, 3-6 x 2-3 µm, one-celled, smooth walled, hyaline.

questions.question: A 51-year-old man on dexamethasone for glioblastoma is admitted with fever and progressively worsening respiratory symptoms over 18 days. CT chest shows multiple non-cavitary nodules measuring 1.5 to 5 cm. He is placed on piperacillin/tazobactam and ciprofloxacin but continues to worsen. After 4 days, respiratory cultures grow dry, yellow colonies, and beaded, filamentous Gram-positive rods are seen on Gram stain.
questions.question_raw: A 51 year-old man, on dexamethasone for a glioblastoma, is admitted with fever and progressively worsening respiratory symptoms x 18 days. CT chest shows multiple non-cavitary nodules measuring 1.5 to 5 cm. Placed on piperacillin/tazobactam and ciprofloxacin, but continues to worsen despite this treatment. After 4 days, respiratory cultures grow dry, yellow colonies. Beaded, filamentous Gram-positive rods are seen on Gram stain.

parts.text: What is the pathogen?
What is the most important next test?
What are three other Gram-positive rods that can grow aerobically that can cause a similar clinical picture?

parts_raw.text: a) What is the pathogen?
b) What is the most important next test?
c) What are three other Gram-positive rods that can grow aerobically that can cause a similar clinical picture?

questions.model_answer: a) Nocardia species. b) Modified acid-fast stain (modified Kinyoun) — Nocardia is partially acid-fast whereas the main mimic Actinomyces is not; this confirms the presumptive diagnosis. c) (1) Rhodococcus; (2) Gordonia; (3) Tsukamurella (also Streptomyces/Actinomadura).

cohort_answer.text:
a) What is the pathogen? - Nocardia spp
b) What is the most important next test? - Modified Acid fast staining - main DDx = Actinomyces which does not stain with modified acid fast but nocardia does (CT head if you already have identified the pathogen) [source note: Uptodate]
c) What are three other Gram-positive rods that can grow aerobically that can cause a similar clinical picture? - Rhodococcus, Gordonia, Tsukumeullea, Streptomyces - also GPB but not pathogenic so wouldn't include in this answer but FYI
cohort_answer.source: AB 2019 (answer slides (with Gram stain and Acid-Fast Staining images interspersed); speaker notes citing Uptodate for part b)
